verses.zh: 以色列家啊，要听我为你们所作的哀歌：
verses.en: Listen to this funeral song I am ready to sing about you,[NOTE:1] family[NOTE:2] of Israel:
notes: Heb “Listen to this word which I am about to take up against you, a funeral song.”
Heb “house.”
verses.commentary:
5:1 "Hear" See note at Amos 3:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣

NASB, REB, NJB, JPSOA
"dirge"

NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta, LXX
"lamentation"

TEV, NET
"funeral song"

This is a specialized poetic structure that is found in Amos 5:2-6 and
Amos 5:16-17. This Hebrew word "dirge" (BDB 884, KB 1097) refers to a particular poetic beat pattern of 3-2, 3-2
(e.g. 2 Sam. 1:19-27; 3:33-34). It is used quite extensively in the book of Lamentations. This form
characterized funeral songs or chants (cf. Amos 5:16-17, 18-20). These songs were an expected
part of the funeral service.

▣ "O house of Israel" The term "house" (BDB 108) is used in the sense of family or
descendants (cf. Amos 1:4,5; 7:9). The phrase "house of Israel" is used several times by Amos
(cf. Amos 5:1,3,4,25; 6:1,14; 7:10,16; 9:9) to refer to the Northern Ten Tribes that split off from Judah in
922 B.C.. in the reign of Rehoboam because of forced labor and heavy taxation. These
breakaway tribes took for themselves the name of the father of the Hebrew tribes "Israel" (Jacob).

Twice in Amos the phrase "house of Jacob" is used (cf. Amos 3:13; 9:8). It if often difficult to
know if Amos is referring only to the northern tribes or if he is addressing all the descendants of Jacob/Israel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

verses.zh: 以色列民（原文是处女）跌倒，不得再起；躺在地上，无人搀扶。
verses.en: “The virgin[NOTE:1] Israel has fallen down and will not get up again.She is abandoned on her own land with no one to help her get up.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “young lady.” The term “Israel” is an appositional genitive.
Or “with no one to lift her up.”
verses.commentary:
5:2 "she has fallen" This (BDB 656, KB 709, Qal PERFECT) is a PROPHETIC
PERFECT that describes something that will happen in the future as if it has already occurred. The term
was used of death in battle (e.g. Jer. 9:22; 46:12; Lam. 2:21; Hosea 7:7).

▣ "she will not rise again" There are two VERBS:

- "no more" (BDB 414, KB 418 is a Hiphil IMPERFECT)

- "to rise" (BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

YHWH's judgment on Israel's eclectic religion is total, complete, once-and-for-all judgment (cf. Amos 4:11; 7:9).

However, this very same VERB is used in Amos 9:11(twice) to promise a restoration of the
royal house of Judah (i.e. "the fallen booth of David"). So again, the theological issue is:

- YHWH's message presented in contrasting black and white truths (dialectic paradoxes)

- chapter 9 refers only to Judah, not Israel

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

▣ "the virgin Israel" This term is parallel with "house of Israel." YHWH took special
care and provided protection for them, like an unmarried daughter (cf. Jer. 14:17) or bride to be (cf. Jer. 18:13; 31:4,21).
This reflects the marriage imagery for YHWH as husband and His covenant people as wife (e.g. Isa. 54:5;
Hosea 2:19; Eph. 5:22-33). The later rabbis saw the wilderness wandering period as their honeymoon
(cf. Jer. 2:2-3; Hosea 2:16). But now the context is of the rape and death of Israel by Assyrian invasion.

For more information on this idiom, see Jer. 46:11 online at
www.freebiblecommentary.org.

▣ "She lies neglected on her land" The VERB (BDB 643, KB 695,
Niphal PERFECT) means forsaken, abandoned to plunder. The land of promise is
now the place of judgment.

There is a very interesting article in NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 522-524, on the theological
aspect of "the land" as YHWH's gift to the descendants of Abraham (cf. Gen. 12:3; 15:12-21). Many of the Mosaic
statutes are based on this concept. This is the reason why cheating fellow covenant brothers out of their
family/tribal inheritance was so offensive to YHWH. YHWH's concern for the land can be seen in "the Sabbath
Year" and "Jubilee Year" regulations. These wealthy land grabbers had totally ignored or willfully rejected
the theological basis of YHWH's ownership and division of the Promised Land (ie. Josh. 12-19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL II. C.

▣ "There is none to raise her up" This is the same VERBAL (BDB 877, KB 1086,
Hiphil PARTICIPLE) used earlier in the verse (Qal INFINITIVE
CONSTRUCT). It seems to be a sarcastic allusion to the inability of the Canaanite gods (whom Israel
worshiped) to rescue her from YHWH's judgment (cf. Amos 5:6). The powerlessness, the non-existence of
Canaanite deities is ridiculed!

verses.zh: 主耶和华如此说：以色列家的城发出一千兵的，只剩一百；发出一百的，只剩十个。
verses.en: The Sovereign Lord says this:“The city that marches out with a thousand soldiers[NOTE:1] will have only a hundred left;the town[NOTE:2] that marches out with a hundred soldiers[NOTE:3] will have only ten left for the family of Israel.”[NOTE:4]
notes: The word “soldiers” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

Heb “The one.” The word “town” has been used in the translation in keeping with the relative sizes of the armed contingents sent out by each. It is also possible that this line is speaking of the same city of the previous line. In other words, the contingent sent by that one city would have suffered a ninety percent casualty loss.
The word “soldiers” is supplied in the translation for clarification.

Heb “for/to the house of Israel.” The translation assumes that this is a graphic picture of what is left over for the defense of the nation (NEB, NJB, NASB, NKJV). Others suggest that this phrase completes the introductory formula (“The sovereign Lord says this…”; see v. 4a; NJPS, NIV11). Another option is that the preposition has a vocative force, “O house of Israel” (F. I. Andersen and D. N. Freedman, Amos [AB], 476).
verses.commentary:
5:3 "the Lord God" This title, "Adon YHWH,' appears often in Amos.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ This was one of the covenant curses (the terms "thousands" [BDB 48] and "hundreds" [BDB 547]
were military units). The emphasis in this verse is not on a remnant returning (cf. Isa. 6:13), but on the
extreme military devastation that will occur.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

verses.zh: 耶和华向以色列家如此说：你们要寻求我，就必存活。
verses.en: The Lord says this to the family[NOTE:1] of Israel:“Seek me[NOTE:2] so you can live!
notes: Heb “house.”

The following verses explain what it meant to seek the Lord. Israel was to abandon the mere formalism and distorted view of God and reality that characterized religious activity at the worship sites, as well as the social injustice that permeated Israelite society. Instead the people were to repent and promote justice in the land. This call to seek the Lord echoes the challenge in 4:13 to prepare to meet him as he truly is.
verses.commentary:
5:4 "seek Me" The Hebrew VERB (BDB 205, KB 233) is a Qal IMPERATIVE
(cf. Amos 5:6,14-15). The connotation of the Hebrew phrase "to seek" involved going to a sanctuary,
however, the context of Amos 5:5 demands that we must seek God on an individual, as well as corporate, basis
(cf. Deut. 4:29), not just in religious ritual. Our attitudes, motives, and lifestyle faith are crucial. Basically
this is a call to repentance to those who already knew (covenantal aspect) YHWH (cf. Rev. 3:20). Fellowship with
YHWH demands an ethical life.

In Amos 5:4 Amos says, "Seek the Lord." This same VERB is also found
in Amos 5:14, "seek good and not evil." These three are somewhat parallel. YHWH is said several times to
be good (e.g. Ps. 86:5; 100:5; 106:1; 107:1; 118:1,29). Therefore, seeking "Me" and seeking "good" may refer
to YHWH (notice the second line of Amos 5:14). This same symbolism can be seen in Hosea 8:2-3.

The Hebrew term "seek" has several meanings.

- inquire of

- seek a deity in prayer and worship

- investigate (to know the heart)

- ask or demand

In this context #2 fits best (cf. Deut. 4:29; Hosea 10:12; Isa. 9:13; 31:1; 55:6; 65:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

▣

NASB
"that you may live"

NKJV, NRSV
"and live"

TEV, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta
"and you will live"

NJB
"and you will survive"

REB
"if you would live"

The MT is reflected in NKJV and NRSV. The VERB (BDB 310, KB 309) is a
Qal IMPERATIVE parallel to "seek." The sense of the IMPERATIVE
is seen in the NASB, TEV, and NJB. Israel's survival as a covenant nation is the issue!

This has always been YHWH's desire (i.e. similar to John 10:10)! YHWH is merciful, if they turn
back to Him, He will pardon, restore, and protect (cf. Deut. 30:2-3,10; 32:46,47).

This outburst of mercy is a plea from the heart of YHWH who does not want to destroy
His own covenant people (cf. Hosea 11:8-11). They were meant to reveal Him to the nations!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 不要往伯特利寻求，不要进入吉甲，不要过到别是巴；因为吉甲必被掳掠，伯特利也必归于无有。
verses.en: Do not seek Bethel.[NOTE:1] Do not visit Gilgal.Do not journey down[NOTE:2] to Beer Sheba.For the people of Gilgal[NOTE:3] will certainly be carried into exile,[NOTE:4] and Bethel will become a place where disaster abounds.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Ironically, Israel was to seek after the Lord, but not at Bethel (the name Bethel means “the house of God” in Hebrew).map For location see Map4-G4; Map5-C1; Map6-E3; Map7-D1; Map8-G3.

Heb “cross over.”sn To worship at Beer Sheba, northern worshipers had to journey down (i.e., cross the border) between Israel and Judah. Apparently, the popular religion of Israel for some included pilgrimage to holy sites in the South.
Heb “For Gilgal.” By metonymy the place name “Gilgal” is used instead of referring directly to the inhabitants. The words “the people of” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

That the people of Gilgal would be taken into exile is ironic, for Gilgal was Israel’s first campsite when the people entered the land under Joshua and the city became a symbol of Israel’s possession of the promised land.tn In the Hebrew text the statement is emphasized by sound play. The name “Gilgal” sounds like the verb גָּלָה (galah, “to go into exile”), which occurs here in the infinitival + finite verb construction (גָּלֹה יִגְלֶה, galoh yigleh). The repetition of the “ג” (g) and “ל” (l) sounds draws attention to the announcement and suggests that Gilgal’s destiny is inherent in its very name.

Heb “disaster,” or “nothing”; cf. NIV “Bethel will be reduced to nothing.”sn Again there is irony. The name Bethel means “house of God” in Hebrew. How surprising and tragic that Bethel, the “house of God” where Jacob received the inheritance given to Abraham, would be overrun by disaster.
verses.commentary:
5:5 "Bethel. . .Gilgal. . .Beersheba" These are all local centers of worship. The first two were in
Israel and the third in southern Judah (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:8; Gen. 21:14, 31; 26:25,33; 46:1) and mentioned earlier in Amos 4:4.

▣ "Beersheba" This was an ancient holy site connected to the Patriarchs (Abraham,
Gen. 21:33; Isaac, Gen. 26:23-25; Jacob, Gen. 28:10; 46:1-7) located in southern Judah.

▣ "For Gilgal will certainly go into captivity" Amos is a skilled poet. Here he uses
a sound play between "Gilgal" and "to go into exile" (BDB 162, KB 191, a Qal INFINITIVE
ABSOLUTE and a Qal IMPERFECT of the same term, which is a grammatical
feature showing intensity). Hebrew poetry is characterized by thought parallelism, multiple meanings of
words, and sound plays.

The exact location of Gilgal is unknown. There seem to be at least two mentioned in the OT. See
fulll notes at Hosea 9:15 and 12:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

▣ "And Bethel will come to trouble" This seems to be a contrast between Bethel
(house of God) and what it had become (house of idolatry [aven, BDB 19], cf. Hosea 4:15; 5:8; 10:5,8).

One of the meanings of "trouble" (aven, BDB 19) can be "idolatry" (i.e. "nothing,"cf. Isa. 41:29; 66:3).

verses.zh: 要寻求耶和华，就必存活，免得他在约瑟家像火发出，在伯特利焚烧，无人扑灭。
verses.en: Seek the Lord so you can live!Otherwise he will break out[NOTE:1] like fire against Joseph’s[NOTE:2] family;[NOTE:3] the fire[NOTE:4] will consume, and no one will be able to quench it and save Bethel.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “rush.” The verb depicts swift movement.
Here Joseph (= Ephraim and Manasseh), as the most prominent of the Israelite tribes, represents the entire northern kingdom.
Heb “house.”
Heb “it”; the referent (the fire mentioned in the previous line) has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “to/for Bethel.” The translation assumes that the preposition indicates advantage, “on behalf of.” Another option is to take the preposition as vocative, “O Bethel.”
verses.commentary:
5:6 "Seek the Lord that you may live" This is parallel to Amos 5:4.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

▣ "He will break forth like a fire" This may be another allusion to Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 4:24). Fire
is imagery for the cleansing power of YHWH or to put it another way, His holiness!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

▣ "O house of Joseph" It is unusual for Israel to be called the "house of Joseph" (cf. Amos 6:6). It
is usually called the "house of Jacob" (or "house of Israel," e.g. Amos 5:1). However, Ephraim and Manasseh,
Joseph's two children, make up the largest land holdings and the most populous tribes of the northern kingdom.

▣

NASB
"for Bethel"

NKJV
"in Bethel"

NRSV, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta
"Bethel"

TEV
"the people of Bethel"

NJB
"at Bethel"

LXX, JPSOA footnote
"the House of Israel"

NEB
"Israel"

The MT has "for Bethel" (NASB). The UBS Text Project, p. 283, gives the MT a "C" rating
(considerable doubt). The NEB follows the LXX, which is a better parallel to "house of Joseph" in the poetic line
before. However, it must be admitted that "Bethel" (i.e. "house of God") is mentioned earlier twice in v. 5, but "the
house of Israel" also occurs in vv. 1,3.

verses.zh: 你们这使公平变为茵蔯、将公义丢弃于地的，
verses.en: The Israelites[NOTE:1] turn justice into bitterness;[NOTE:2] they throw what is fair and right[NOTE:3] to the ground.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “Those who”; the referent (the Israelites) has been specified in the translation for clarity. In light of vv. 11-13, it is also possible that the words are directed at a more limited group within the nation—those with social and economic power.

There is an interesting wordplay here with the verb הָפַךְ (hafakh, “overturn, turn”). Israel “turns” justice into wormwood (cf. 6:12), while the Lord “turns” darkness into morning (v. 8; cf. 4:11; 8:10). Israel’s turning is for evil, whereas the Lord’s is to demonstrate his absolute power and sovereignty.
Heb “they throw righteousness.”

In v. 7 the prophet begins to describe the guilty Israelites but then interrupts his word picture with a parenthetical, yet powerful, description of the judge they must face (vv. 8-9). He resumes his description of the sinners in v. 10.
verses.commentary:
5:7 "for those who turn justice into wormwood" "Justice" is a parallel to "righteousness." These two
terms often appear together in the same context in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 8:15; 1 Kgs. 10:9; 1 Chr. 18:14; 2 Chr. 9:8;
Ps. 99:4; Isa. 1:21; 5:7; 9:7; 28:17; 32:1,16; 33:5; 59:14; Jer. 4:2; 9:24; 22:3,15; 23:5; 33:15; Ezek. 18:5,19,21,27;
33:14,16,19; 45:9; Amos 5:7,24). This is not the "justification by faith," imputed righteousness of the New
Covenant, but the Old Covenant mandate that YHWH wanted a people to fully reveal His character
(cf. Matt. 5:19-20,48). However, sinful fallen mankind, even the covenant people, were unable to live out the
holiness of God!

The PARTICIPLE (BDB 245, KB 253, Qal PARTICIPLE),
when Israel is the subject, is used in a negative sense (cf. Amos 5:7; 6:12; Jer. 2:21). In Amos 4:11 Amos
mentioned Sodom and Gomorrah as being overthrown, using the same root but with YHWH as the subject.

Wormwood (BDB 542) refers to any plant that is bitter (cf. UBS's Fauna and Flora
of the Bible, p. 198). The rich had prevented justice. The legal system was a bitter thing to the poor, not
a haven (cf. Amos 5:12; 6:12). This may be another allusion to idolatry in Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 29:18;
Jer. 9:14; 23:15). The cognate in Arabic means "curse."

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣

NASB
"cast righteousness down to the earth"

NKJV
"lay righteousness to rest in the earth"

NRSV
"bring righteousness to the ground"

TEV
"cheat people out of their rights"

NJB, REB
"throw uprightness to the ground"

Peshitta
"lower righteousness to the ground"

The idea here is to cast down (BDB 245, KB 253, Qal PARTICIPLE)
with a view toward trampling underfoot (cf. Isaiah 28:2-3). Judges, like the king, were to represent YHWH.

Notice that "justice" and "righteousness" are parallel (cf. Amos 5:24; 6:12). There is an
ethical-practical aspect to biblical faith! Biblical faith involves

- personal trust

- godly living

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

verses.zh: 要寻求那造昴星和参星，使死荫变为晨光，使白日变为黑夜，命海水来浇在地上的―耶和华是他的名；
verses.en: But there is one who made the constellations Pleiades and Orion;he can turn the darkness into morningand daylight[NOTE:1] into night.He summons the water of the seasand pours it out on the earth’s surface.The Lord is his name!
notes: Heb “darkens the day into night.”
verses.commentary:
5:8-9 This is a poetic doxology to God (Elohim, Gen. 1:1) as Creator and Judge. There are three of these
wonderful doxologies in Amos (cf. Amos 4: 4; 5:8-9; 9:5-6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

5:8 "the Pleiades" This is literally "heap" or "herd" (BDB 465, KB 472, cf. Job 9:9, 38:31). This was one of the brightest
and most popular of the star clusters (Hesiod calls it "the seven sisters") in the constellation Taurus. The UBS, Translator's Handbook,
pp. 105, 242, asserts that in Palestine its setting below the horizon introduces winter. This then makes the poetic lines refer to God not
as creator only, but active controller (Providence) of the natural order (i.e. Job 9:9).

▣ "Orion" This is literally "fool" (BDB 493, KB 489 II) in the sense of aggressive. It is used to
refer to a rebel. The ancients identified this constellation with Nimrod (the warrior, cf. Gen. 10:8-9). It
was visible in the summer. God controls the seasons (i.e. the order and regularity of the natural
world)! Apparently, God's creation and control of the stars (cf. Gen. 1:14-19) was a necessary theological
statement in the light of astral worship (cf. Amos 5:26).

▣ "changes deep darkness into morning" In context this speaks of God's control of the
heavenly bodies (cf. Ps. 19: 24). This phrase may be parallel in concept to Amos 4:13c.

▣ "Who calls for the waters of the sea" There are several theories as to the meaning of this phrase:

- it refers to the boundaries of the oceans (cf. Gen. 1:9-10)

- it refers to YHWH, not Ba'al, as the source of rain (i.e. a blessing to support growth)

- it is possibly an allusion to the flood (a judgment motif, cf. Genesis 6)

YHWH controls the waters of creation as He does the stars. Water and the planets are the two things in Genesis 1
that are not said to have been spoken into existence by God (i.e. pre-existing material, cf. Gen. 1:2). See John H. Walton, The
Lost World of Genesis One: An Ancient Cosmology.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

▣ "The Lord is His name" The name in Hebrew was very
significant in describing the character of an individual. Israel's God's name, "YHWH," is from Exod. 3:14, from
the Hebrew VERB "to be."

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH (OT)

verses.zh: 他使力强的忽遭灭亡，以致保障遭遇毁坏。
verses.en: He flashes[NOTE:1] destruction down upon the strong so that destruction overwhelms[NOTE:2] the fortified places.
notes: The precise meaning of the Hebrew verb בָּלַג (balag, translated here “flashes”) is uncertain.
Heb “comes upon.” Many prefer to repoint the verb as Hiphil and translate, “he brings destruction upon the fortified places.”
verses.commentary:
5:9

NASB, REB
"flashes forth"

NKJV
"He rains"

NRSV
"flash out"

TEV, NJB
"brings"

The Hebrew term's (BDB 114, KB 132, Hiphil PARTICIPLE)
meaning is in doubt. Its use in Job and the Psalms implies a cheerfulness or joy (meaning of the Arabic
root). However, that meaning does not fit Amos at all unless Amos is speaking sarcastically of YHWH
smiling at the destruction of idolatrous Israel and her military fortifications. The NASB takes its translation
from the possible meaning of the Hiphil, "let something flare up" (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 660).

The UBS Text Project, p. 284, gives a textual emendation that turns v. 9 into the names
for three constellations (i.e. gods).

- bull (BDB 993, KB 1417-1418)

- goat (BDB 736, KB 804)

- vintager (BDB 130, KB 148)

This forms a parallel with the mentioning of "the Pleiades (i.e. "the cluster") and Orion"
(i.e. "the giant") of v. 8.

▣ "the strong" This may refer to the economically and politically powerful (cf. Amos 5:10-13; 2:14).
The opposite of "the poor," the very ones who take advantage of them! However, because of the parallel to
"fortresses," it may refer to the Israeli military. Also see note above for a connection to constellations.

verses.zh: 你们怨恨那在城门口责备人的，憎恶那说正直话的。
verses.en: The Israelites[NOTE:1] hate anyone who arbitrates at the city gate;[NOTE:2] they despise anyone who speaks honestly.
notes: Heb “they”; the referent (the Israelites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
In ancient Israelite culture, legal disputes were resolved in the city gate, where the town elders met.
verses.commentary:
5:10 "They hate him who reproves in the gate" Those (honest judges, true witnesses) who tried to
stand up and defend the poor and helpless (exactly who this refers to is uncertain, some kind of legal advocate)
were vehemently attacked by the status quo leadership (cf. Isa. 59:14-15). This is another allusion to Deuteronomy's
cursing and blessing section (cf. Deut. 27:25).

The gate was the place of justice in the ancient Near East (cf. Deut. 25:1-3; Ruth 4:1-12). This is where
the elders of the communities sat to hear and judicate the issues of the community (cf. Deut. 19:12; 21:3,8,19; 21:3,8; 22:15;
25:7-8). These elders and judges are addressed directly by Amos in vv. 10-17.

For a good brief discussion of Israel's judicial system, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 152-157.

▣ "abhor" This (BDB 1073, KB 1765, Piel IMPERFECT) is a strong
VERB, often used to denote YHWH's rejection of idolatry. It is parallel to "hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338,
Qal PERFECT) in this same verse.

▣

NASB
"integrity"

NKJV, Peshitta
"uprightly"

NRSV, NJB
"the truth"

TEV
"the whole truth"

REB
"nothing less than the truth"

JPSOA
"just"

The term's (BDB 1071, KB 1748) basic meaning is to be exact or straight. This imagery for
moral/ethical uprightness was derived from the word for a palm tree. Notice its usage.

- Noah, Gen. 6:9

- Abraham, Gen. 17:1

- peace offerings, Lev. 22:21

- godly Israelites, Deut. 18:13; Prov. 2:7; 10:9

- God, Deut. 32:4 2 Sam. 22:31,33; Ps. 18; 30,32

- Job, Job 1:1,8; 2:3

- God's word, Ps. 19:7

SPECIAL TOPIC: BLAMELESS, INNOCENT, GUILTLESS, WITHOUT REPROACH, B. 2. b.

5:11a-b The first two poetic lines of this verse document some of the abuses of the poor:

- the options for understanding 11a are

- heavy rent (i.e. taken from Akkadian root, NASB, NET, REB, JPSOA)

- trample on (i.e. taken from Hebrew root "to trample" [BDB 143, KB 165, Poel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT],
cf. NASB (margin), NKJV, NRSV, NJB)

- the LXX and Peshitta understand it as a physical blow by the rich to the poor (i.e. possibly imagery for a tax)

- a tax on food

- bribery at the gate (cf. Amos 5:12)

The term poor (see note at Amos 2:7) may refer to "peasant farmers" (see note at NIDOTTE,
vol. 1, p. 951).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUNGER

5:11c-e This is another curse for violation of the Mosaic Covenant (cf. Deut. 28:30,39). The rich
had built luxurious homes ("well-hewn stone"; also note Amos 3:15) by exploiting the poor (cf. Amos 5:11-12). But
YHWH would not let them live with their ill gotten gain (cf. Micah 6:15; Zeph. 1:13). This is an allusion to the Assyrian exile.

verses.zh: 你们践踏贫民，向他们勒索麦子；你们用凿过的石头建造房屋，却不得住在其内；栽种美好的葡萄园，却不得喝所出的酒。
verses.en: Therefore, because you make the poor pay taxes on their crops[NOTE:1] and exact a grain tax from them,you will not live in the houses you built with chiseled stone,nor will you drink the wine from the fine[NOTE:2] vineyards you planted.[NOTE:3]
notes: Traditionally, “because you trample on the poor” (cf. KJV, ASV, NAB, NIV84, NRSV, NLT). The traditional view derives the verb from בּוּס (bus, “to trample”; cf. Isa. 14:25), but more likely it is cognate to an Akkadian verb meaning “to exact an agricultural tax” (see H. R. Cohen, Biblical Hapax Legomena [SBLDS], 49; S. M. Paul, Amos [Hermeneia], 172-73) (cf. NIV11 “you levy a straw tax on the poor” ).
Or “lovely”; cf. KJV, NASB, NRSV “pleasant,” NAB “choice,” NIV “lush.”
Heb “Houses of chiseled stone you built, but you will not live in them. Fine vineyards you planted, but you will not drink their wine.”

verses.zh: 我知道你们的罪过何等多，你们的罪恶何等大。你们苦待义人，收受贿赂，在城门口屈枉穷乏人。
verses.en: Certainly[NOTE:1] I am aware of[NOTE:2] your many rebellious acts[NOTE:3] and your numerous sins.You[NOTE:4] torment the innocent, you take bribes,and you deny justice to[NOTE:5] the needy at the city gate.[NOTE:6]
notes: Or “for.”
Or “I know” (so most English versions).
Or “transgressions,” “sins.” See the note on the word “crimes” in 1:3 and on the phrase “covenant violations” in 2:4.
Heb “Those who.”
Heb “turn aside.” They “turn aside” the needy by denying them the justice they deserve at the city gate (where legal decisions were made, and therefore where justice should be done).
Legal disputes were resolved in the city gate, where the town elders met.
verses.commentary:
5:12 This verse, like Amos 5:10-11, lists the sins of the wealthy class against the poor (possibly
small farmers) and underprivileged. These are the very ones the ethical God cares about because of their
helplessness and vulnerability (cf. Deut. 10:18; 14:29; 16:11; 24:17-22; 26:12-13; 27:19). This is another
Deuteronomic emphasis. The prophets always looked back to the Mosaic Covenant (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT]).

The term translated "bribe" (BDB 497 I, KB 495 IV, cf. Exod. 23:8; Deut. 16:19; 27:25; 1 Sam. 12:3;
Prov. 6:35) is the same term used to describe God's "covering," "atoning" for sin (KB 493). This important theological
term is used here in a derived sense of covering someone's hand or eyes. It is a shocking use of a wonderful
theological term.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

verses.zh: 所以通达人见这样的时势必静默不言，因为时势真恶。
verses.en: For this reason whoever is smart[NOTE:1] keeps quiet[NOTE:2] in such a time,for it is an evil[NOTE:3] time.
notes: Or “the wise”; or “the prudent.” Another option is to translate “the successful, prosperous” and understand this as a reference to the rich oppressors. See G. V. Smith, Amos, 169-70. In this case the following verb will also have a different nuance, that is, the wealthy remain silent before the abuses they perpetuate. See the note on the verb translated “keeps quiet” later in this verse.

Or “moans, laments,” from a homonymic verbal root. If the rich oppressors are in view, then the verb (whether translated “will be silenced” or “will lament”) describes the result of God’s judgment upon them. See G. V. Smith, Amos, 170.
If this is a judgment announcement against the rich, then the Hebrew phrase עֵת רָעָה (ʿet raʿah) must be translated, “[a] disastrous time.” See G. V. Smith, Amos, 170.
verses.commentary:
5:13 This is a very difficult verse because it seems to go against all that the prophet himself
advocates and practices. This again may be a play on the semantic field of the PARTICIPLE,
"he who is prudent" (BDB 968, KB 1328, Hiphil PARTICIPLE). The Hiphil can mean

- look at (to make one wise, cf. Gen. 3:6)

- give attention to (e.g. Deut. 32:29)

- have comprehension (e.g. Dan. 1:4; 9:25)

- give insight, teach (e.g. Dan. 9:22; 11:33,35)

- act prudently (e.g. Amos 5:13)

- prosper (e.g. Isa. 52:13; Jer. 10:21)

- cause to prosper (e.g. Deut. 29:9)

A good example of how this term can mean #5 or #6/#7 see Jer. 23:5. If so the one used here
may be another allusion to Deuteronomy (i.e. Deut. 29:9). They were meant to prosper in YHWH's blessing
(cf. Deuteronomy 27-29), but they were prospering because they were breaking Moses' Covenant in
their treatment of the powerless of their society.

It is also possible (UBS, Handbook, pp. 106-109) to see the key to the structure
related to the two people addressed in Amos 5:10.

- "they hate. . .they abhor" (v. 10), this group is addressed in Amos 5:11-12

- "who reproves. . .who speaks with integrity" (v. 10), these were addressed in Amos 5:13

verses.zh: 你们要求善，不要求恶，就必存活。这样，耶和华―万军之　神必照你们所说的与你们同在。
verses.en: Seek good and not evil so you can live!Then the Lord God of Heaven’s Armies just might be with you, as you claim he is.
verses.commentary:
5:14 "Seek good and not evil" Note the prophet's sharp contrasts (cf. Amos 5:15). There is a choice
to be made which has eternal consequences. "Seek" (BDB 205, KB 233, Qal IMPERATIVE)
is another IMPERATIVE. Notice this IMPERATIVE'S relationship with those
in Amos 5:4, 6 that emphasize ethical lifestyles. It must be remembered that biblical faith has two foci:

- personal relationship (cf. John 3:16; Romans 4)

- deeds of love (cf. 1 Corinthians 13; Eph. 2:8-10 and 1 John 3:23)

Amos admonishes Israel to "seek good." Isaiah
uses the same VERB to admonish God's people to seek justice (cf. Isa. 1:17). What do we care
about, strive for, seek after? The answer to this question tells us who we are and who we serve!

▣ "the Lord God of hosts be with you" This is the greatest
promise that God can make (cf. Ps. 23). The title "Lord God of Hosts" has
two related meanings in the OT:

- YHWH as commander of the angelic army

- YHWH as controller of the astral bodies that represent angelic powers (Babylonian idolatry)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

▣ "Just as you have said" Amos may have been referring to

- a common teaching of the priests/Levites

- an often used liturgy/psalm

- the recurrent claim that Israel was the covenant-chosen people (e.g. Exod. 19:5-6; Deut. 7:6; 14:2)

verses.zh: 要恶恶好善，在城门口秉公行义；或者耶和华―万军之　神向约瑟的余民施恩。
verses.en: Hate what is wrong, love what is right.Promote[NOTE:1] justice at the city gate.[NOTE:2] Maybe the Lord God of Heaven’s Armies will have mercy on[NOTE:3] those who are left from[NOTE:4] Joseph.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “set up, establish.” In the ancient Near East it was the responsibility especially of the king to establish justice. Here the prophet extends that demand to local leaders and to the nation as a whole (cf. 5:24).
Legal disputes were resolved in the city gate (see the note in v. 12). This repetition of this phrase serves to highlight a deliberate contrast to the injustices cited in vv. 11-13.
Or “will show favor to.”
Or “the remnant of” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV); cf. CEV “what’s left of your people.”
Joseph (= Ephraim and Manasseh), as the most prominent of the Israelite tribes, represents the entire northern kingdom.
verses.commentary:
5:15 "Hate evil, love good,

And establish justice in the gate" These are three Hebrew IMPERATIVES:

- "hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338, Qal IMPERATIVE)

- "love" (BDB 12, KB 17, Qal IMPERATIVE)

- "establish" (BDB 426, KB 427, Hiphil IMPERATIVE)

These reflect the covenant of Moses. Notice that for Amos there is no distinction
between the secular and the sacred, between the heart and the hand (cf. Micah 6:8). YHWH's people must
reflect YHWH's character!

The command "establish" has the connotation of specific, purposeful action (e.g. Hosea 2:3). YHWH's
faithful must determine in their hearts and minds that justice, fairness, and integrity will prevail in their sphere
of influence.

▣ "Perhaps the Lord. . .May be gracious to the remnant of
Joseph" The prophet is asserting a limited hope (i.e. "perhaps" BDB 19) for those few Israelites who
would repent and live out their faith (i.e. "seek Me," Amos 5:4; "seek the Lord," Amos 5:6).

For "remnant" see SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

verses.zh: 主耶和华―万军之　神如此说：在一切宽阔处必有哀号的声音；在各街市上必有人说：哀哉！哀哉！又必叫农夫来哭号，叫善唱哀歌的来举哀。
verses.en: Because of Israel’s sins[NOTE:1] this is what the Lord, the Lord God of Heaven’s Armies,[NOTE:2] says:“In all the squares there will be wailing;in all the streets they will mourn the dead.[NOTE:3] They will tell the field workers[NOTE:4] to lamentand the professional mourners[NOTE:5] to wail.
notes: Heb “Therefore.” This logical connector relates back to the accusation of vv. 10-13, not to the parenthetical call to repentance in vv. 14-15. To indicate this clearly, the phrase “Because of Israel’s sins” is used in the translation.
Or “the Lord.” The Hebrew term translated “sovereign One” here is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).

Heb “they will say, ‘Ah! Ah!’” The Hebrew term הוֹ (ho, “ah, woe”) is an alternate form of הוֹי (hoy), a word used to mourn the dead and express outwardly one’s sorrow. See 1 Kgs 13:30; Jer 22:18; 34:5. This wordplay follows quickly, as v. 18 begins with הוֹי (“woe”).
Or “farmers” (NIV, NCV, NRSV, TEV, CEV, NLT).
Heb “those who know lamentation.”sn Professional mourners are referred to elsewhere in the OT (2 Chr 35:25; Jer 9:17) and ancient Near Eastern literature. See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 180.
verses.commentary:
5:16 "Therefore" This relates to Amos 5:10-13. It does not relate to the repeated admonition
to repent, begun in Amos 5:4-6 (key word, "seek").

▣ "There is wailing in all the plazas. . .'Alas! Alas'" The prophet began the funeral
dirge in Amos 5:1; now judgment has come and everybody is wailing.

"Plazas" would be parallel to "gates" or "markets." Even the term "streets" (BDB 299)
can mean plaza or market (e.g. 1 Kgs. 20:34).

▣ "farmer" I believe "farmer" is the referent to "the poor." It was not the poor as in modern,
western cultures, but the small farmer on ancestral land (given by lot, YHWH, Joshua 12-19) who were being exploited. The
Mosaic stipulations of the Sabbath Year and the Jubilee Year were being ignored and land was permanently taken.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, II. B., C.

▣ "professional mourners" Near Eastern people are very expressive in their mourning rites. There
were trained people available to help in this cultural grieving process (cf. 2 Chr. 35:25; Jer. 9:17). See James M.
Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible, pp. 283-284.

verses.zh: 在各葡萄园必有哀号的声音，因为我必从你中间经过。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: In all the vineyards there will be wailing,for I will pass through[NOTE:1] your midst,” says the Lord.
notes: The expression pass through your midst alludes to Exod 12:12, where the Lord announced he would “pass through” Egypt and bring death to the Egyptian firstborn.
verses.commentary:
5:17 "I will pass through the midst of you" This same phrase is used in Exod. 12:12 for the Death Angel
passing through Egypt in judgment on the night of Passover. YHWH's coming could be for blessing or judgment
(cf. Amos 5:18). Israel viewed it as a certain blessing, but Amos revealed that it would be for judgment. What an
ironic, tragic reversal (cf. Amos 5:18-20)! All humans made in God's image sense their need for Him (cf. Amos 5:14b). He
wants to be with us, but our actions necessitate judgment, not fellowship!

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEATH ANGEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

verses.zh: 想望耶和华日子来到的有祸了！你们为何想望耶和华的日子呢？那日黑暗没有光明，
verses.en: Woe[NOTE:1] to those who wish for the day of the Lord!Why do you want the Lord’s day of judgment to come?It will bring darkness, not light.
notes: The term הוֹי (hoy, “woe”) was used when mourning the dead (see the note on the word “dead” in 5:16). The prophet here either engages in role playing and mourns the death of the nation in advance or sarcastically taunts those who hold to this misplaced belief.
verses.commentary:
5:18 "Alas" This is literally "woe" (BDB 222). This is an interjection of grief and mourning over
the dead (cf. Amos 5:16; Jer. 22:18; 34:5). See full note at Amos 6:1.

▣ "you who are longing for the day of the Lord" This VERB
(BDB 16, KB 20, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) means "desire for yourselves." These people thought
YHWH's coming (i.e. "the day of the Lord") would bring blessings and deliverance
because they were covenant people (cf. Amos 3:2). But because of this very reason, judgment would come (cf. Romn. 9:4-5).
Because of the blindness of their hearts, YHWH was coming to them as Judge (cf. Amos 3:14; 5:18; 8:3,9,11,13), not Savior
(cf. Amos 9:11,13). Their religion resulted in a curse (cf. Lev. 26 and Deut. 27-29).

Amos is the first of the writing prophets and this is the first use of the phrase "the Day of
the Lord" (see note at Amos 2:16). It is also used often by Joel (cf. Joel 1:15; 2:1,11,31; 3:14).
It may have been imagery from the days of "Holy War" (i.e. Joshua and Judges). YHWH was the ever-present provider and
protector of His covenant people, but in days of conflict His physical manifestation in miraculous ways delivered His people from
danger. However, Israel had so violated the covenant that its privilege had turned to judgment and rejection (cf. Joel 2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣ "It will be darkness and not light" This continues the contrast on these terms (cf. Amos 4:13c; 5:8c,20).

- darkness (BDB 365)

- light (BDB 21)

SPECIAL TOPIC: DARKNESS, I.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIGHT

verses.zh: 景况好像人躲避狮子又遇见熊，或是进房屋以手靠墙，就被蛇咬。
verses.en: Disaster will be inescapable,[NOTE:1] as if a man ran from a lion only to meet a bear, then escaped into[NOTE:2] a house, leaned his hand against the wall, and was bitten by a poisonous snake.
notes: The words “Disaster will be inescapable” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “went” (so KJV, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
5:19 There is absolutely no place to flee from YHWH's judgment (i.e. Job 20:24; Isa. 24:17-18; Jer. 15:2-3).

▣ "lion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

verses.zh: 耶和华的日子不是黑暗没有光明吗？不是幽暗毫无光辉吗？
verses.en: Don’t you realize the Lord’s day of judgment will bring[NOTE:1] darkness, not light—gloomy blackness, not bright light?
notes: Heb “Will not the day of the Lord be.”
verses.commentary:
5:20 What irony! What tragedy!

▣ "with no brightness in it" The "brightness" (BDB 618 I, KB 667 I ) may be an allusion to the glory of God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

verses.zh: 我厌恶你们的节期，也不喜悦你们的严肃会。
verses.en: “I absolutely despise[NOTE:1] your festivals!I get no pleasure[NOTE:2] from your religious assemblies.
notes: Heb “I hate”; “I despise.”

Heb “I will not smell.” These verses are full of vivid descriptions of the Lord’s total rejection of Israelite worship. In the first half of this verse two verbs are used together for emphasis. Here the verb alludes to the sense of smell, a fitting observation since offerings would have been burned on the altar ideally to provide a sweet aroma to God (see, e.g., Lev 1:9, 13, 17; Num 29:36). Other senses that are mentioned include sight and hearing in vv. 22-23.
verses.commentary:
5:21-24 Do these verses show that YHWH rejects the sacrificial system given in Leviticus 1-7? There
are many strong passages in the Prophets that show YHWH's displeasure at His people's practice of the sacrificial
system (cf. Isa. 1:11-17; Jer. 6:20; 7:21-23; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21-27; Micah 6:6-8). The sacrificial system was YHWH's
way of dealing with human sin so as to develop and continue a personal, loving, trusting relationship with His
highest creation. The problem was not the Mosaic Covenant and sacrifice, but human abuses of it. However, Israel not
only turned it into mere ritual and form, but even merged it with pagan practices.

- YHWH wants fellowship!

- YHWH wants a people who reflect His character!

- YHWH wants to reach all humans through the witness of a chosen group (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5-6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

5:21 "I hate, I reject your festivals,

Nor do I delight in your solemn assemblies" These are strong terms! They were very religious
(i.e. Amos 4:4-5), but their attitudes and hearts were far from God (cf. Isa. 6:9-10. Their religiosity was an abomination to
God (cf. Isa. 29:13)! The first two VERBS, "I hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338) and "I reject" (BDB 549, KB 540) are
Qal PERFECTS, which denote a settled, complete attitude.

The term "festivals" (BDB 290, KB 290) is often used to denote the three major annual feasts
(cf. Exod. 23:15-16; Lev. 23). These were required feasts for all males.

The term "delight" (BDB 926, KB 1280, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is literally
"smell," which refers to the Mosaic phrase "soothing aroma," denoting YHWH's acceptance of a sacrifice
(e.g. Gen. 8:21; Exod. 29:18,25; Lev. 26:31; 1 Sam. 26:19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, I. D. #1-3

SPECIAL TOPIC: A SOOTHING AROMA

verses.zh: 你们虽然向我献燔祭和素祭，我却不悦纳，也不顾你们用肥畜献的平安祭；
verses.en: Even if you offer me burnt and grain offerings,[NOTE:1] I will not be satisfied;I will not look with favor on your peace offerings of fattened calves.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “burnt offerings and your grain offerings.”
Heb “Peace offering[s], your fattened calves, I will not look at.”
verses.commentary:
5:22 Religiosity without relationship is an abomination (cf. Amos 4:4-5; Isa. 1: 10-20; Jer. 7). YHWH does not reject
the sacrificial system, but its inappropriate use (ritual without repentant faith; form without appropriate attitude and lifestyle action)!

▣ "I will not even look" "Look" (BDB 613, KB 661, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is
used in the sense of accept or acknowledge.

▣ "fatlings" This (BDB 597, KB 635) refers to specially cared for young animals which were raised to be sacrificed.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURNT OFFERINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRAIN OFFERINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE OFFERINGS

verses.zh: 要使你们歌唱的声音远离我，因为我不听你们弹琴的响声。
verses.en: Take away from me your[NOTE:1] noisy songs;I don’t want to hear the music of your stringed instruments.[NOTE:2]
notes: In this verse the second person suffixes are singular and not plural like they are in vv. 21-22 and vv. 25-27. Some have suggested that perhaps a specific individual or group within the nation is in view.
The Hebrew word probably refers to “harps” (NASB, NIV, NRSV) or “lutes” (NEB).
verses.commentary:
5:23 "take away from Me the noise of your songs" This (BDB 693, KB 747) is a Hiphil IMPERATIVE
MASCULINE SINGULAR. Even sacred, glorious music without the proper motive is a farce, hypocrisy, and
an abomination to God. God desires faith, not only form!

This verse does show that the northern tribes adopted the worship forms (i.e. music by the guilds,
cf. 1 Sam. 10:5) of the temple in Jerusalem (developed by David, cf. 2 Sam. 6:5,15). The leaders (Jeroboam I) wanted
these northern altars (i.e. Dan and Bethel) to duplicate the worship techniques so that the common people would not sense a difference.

It is surprising that the VERBS are SINGULAR. It is just possible
that in Amos 5:23 Amos is addressing the high priest at Bethel.

▣

NASB, NRSV, TEV, NIV, Peshitta
"harps"

NKJV, NET
"stringed instruments"

NJB
"lyres"

REV, JPSOA
"lutes"

LXX
"instruments"

As the number of English translations demonstrates, moderns do not know to what type
of stringed instrument this refers (BDB 614, KB 664 II). To note the number of other instruments it is often associated with see
2 Sam. 6:5 and Ps. 92:3. It is possible that Assyrian wall pictures have depicted this instrument as strings with
a sounding box, something like our bass fiddle. See James M. Freeman, Manners and Customs of the Bible
pp. 221-222.

verses.zh: 惟愿公平如大水滚滚，使公义如江河滔滔。
verses.en: Justice must flow like torrents of water,righteous actions[NOTE:1] like a stream that never dries up.
notes: Traditionally, “righteousness.”
verses.commentary:
5:24 This is one of the most famous verses in Amos. YHWH desires His people to focus on who He is, not
on certain worship days, but on every day. True faith is what we are, not what we do; but who we are will be clearly
seen in what we do, how we do it, and why we do it (cf. Matt. 7; Eph. 1:4; 2:10).

"Justice" and "righteousness" are parallel, as in Amos 5:7. In this context they refer to human
obedience to the Mosaic Covenant lived out in a proper relationship between God and godly living.

The VERB "roll down" (BDB 146, KB 193) is a Niphal JUSSIVE,
which denotes an IMPERATIVE sense.

▣ "an ever-flowing stream" This (BDB 450, KB 44) refers to a spring that never runs dry (i.e. is not seasonal). It
is a powerful imagery for a life of active faith (cf. Jer. 22:3; Ezek. 45:9; Micah 6:8).

verses.zh: 「以色列家啊，你们在旷野四十年，岂是将祭物和供物献给我呢？
verses.en: You did not bring me[NOTE:1] sacrifices and grain offerings during the 40 years you spent in the wilderness, family[NOTE:2] of Israel.
notes: Heb “Did you bring me…?” This rhetorical question expects a negative answer. The point seems to be this: Since sacrifices did not characterize God’s relationship with Israel during the nation’s formative years, the people should not consider them to be so fundamental. The Lord places a higher priority on justice than he does on empty ritual.sn Like Jer 7:22-23, this passage seems to contradict the Pentateuchal accounts that indicate Israel did offer sacrifices during the wilderness period. It is likely that both Amos and Jeremiah overstate the case to emphasize the relative insignificance of sacrifices in comparison to weightier matters of the covenant. See R. de Vaux, Ancient Israel, 428.
Heb “house.”
verses.commentary:
5:25 This is a very difficult verse to interpret. It can be a question or an affirmation (cf. TEV). There have been two lines of interpretation:

- Amos is asserting that the children of Israel did not sacrifice in the wilderness (cf. Jer. 7:21-22 and NJB)

- although they did sacrifice in a limited (JB) way, the object of their sacrifice was not YHWH, but Assyrian
gods who were leading them (sarcasm) into exile.

verses.zh: 你们抬着为自己所造之摩洛的帐幕和偶像的龛，并你们的神星。
verses.en: You will pick up your images[NOTE:1] of Sikkuth,[NOTE:2] your king,[NOTE:3] and Kiyyun,[NOTE:4] your star god, which you made for yourselves,
notes: This word appears in an awkward position in the Hebrew, following “Kiyyun.” It is placed here for better sense.

The Hebrew term סִכּוּת (sikkut) apparently refers to Sakkuth, a Mesopotamian star god identified with Ninurta in an Ugaritic god list. The name is vocalized in the Hebrew text after the pattern of שִׁקּוּץ (shiqquts, “detestable thing”). See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 195-96. Some English versions, following the LXX, translate as “tent” or “shrine” (NEB, NIV), pointing the term as סֻכַּת (sukkat; cf. 9:11).
LXX, Vulgate, and Acts 7:43 read “Moloch” (cf. KJV). The Hebrew consonants are the same for both “king” and “Moloch” (מֹלֶךְ; molekh).

The Hebrew term כִּיּוּן (kiyyun) apparently refers to the Mesopotamian god Kayamanu, or Saturn. The name, like “Sikkuth” in the previous line, is vocalized in the Hebrew text after the pattern of שִׁקּוּץ (shiqquts, “detestable thing”). See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 195-96. Some versions translate as “pedestal” (NEB, NIV), relating the term to the root כּוּן (kun).
verses.commentary:
5:26 There is much discussion on the time element of this verse. Does it refer to the forty years of
wilderness wandering of Amos 5:25 or does it refer to the future wanderings of the Assyrian exile? It seems
that because the idols mentioned are Assyrian star gods (i.e. Akkadian names for Saturn) this verse is referring
to current time, while Amos 5:25 refers to the wilderness wanderings after the Exodus from Egypt.

Another possibility is that Israel had made the sacrificial system ultimate when in fact they
could not perform it after they left Egypt for many years (no tabernacle). During those years personal trust in
God's care, presence, and provision was the focus of their faith, not sacrifice. This does not depreciate the
sacrificial system. It was surely the will of God, but God Himself was the goal, not the ritual, liturgy, and
cultus! Motive and attitude were crucial!

Just a note about Stephen's quote of Amos 5:25-27 in Acts 7:42-43. Most Jews of the first
century A.D. used the Septuagint translation of the OT. In some places it follows a different
Hebrew text from the Masoretic Text. This is a problem! However, even in the Dead Sea Scrolls both traditions are
present. None of the verses affect the truth or trustworthiness of doctrine or practice. We must realize that
Christianity does not stand or fall on difference between the Hebrew OT and its ancient versions or NT
manuscript variation. See a discussion of this in Gleason Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp 381-382.

▣ "Sikkuth your king" The MT has "Sakkuth" (BDB 696, KB 753), meaning uncertain because apparently
Jewish scribes substituted vowels from derogatory terms. The LXX has "booth of" or "tabernacle of," however, this term is
found in Assyrian documents to refer to a war god named Adar-Melek, which refers to Saturn (Ninurta in Ugaritic). Notice a deity is called "king,"
which shows the cultural background for YHWH as king.

▣

"the pedestal"

This also refers to an Assyrian star god, who is also identified with the planet Saturn
(BDB 475). The NASB reflects the Hebrew spelling which is a combination of the consonants of the name
of the star god, but the vowels from the Hebrew word "abominations" (BDB 1055, JPSOA footnote). This was a
common way for Hebrew scribes to ridicule the names of gods, kings, and nations (e.g. Sikkuth).

The spelling "Kaiwan" is from Akkadian or Arabic root.

The translation of the term as "pedestal" supposes that the term comes from the root,
"to be firm" (kwn).

The JPSOA suggests that vv. 26-27 would fit well after Amos 6:14.

verses.commentary:
5:27 "I will make you go into exile beyond Damascus" This refers to the Assyrian exile, which
occurred in 722 B.C. after a three year siege of Samaria (cf. possibly Amos 4:3; and Hosea 9:3;
10:6; 11:5). This again is an allusion to the cursings and blessings section of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29.

▣ "says the Lord, whose name is God of hosts" One of the
names for Israel's God is "YHWH of hosts" or "YHWH Sabaoth" (cf. 1 Sam. 1:3). In this text Elohim is
substituted for YHWH (cf. Ps. 80:7,14,19). Here, the title is connected to God as the controller of a heavenly army
(i.e. the stars). YHWH, not astral deities (i.e. Assyrian star gods), was Israel's hope!

The worship of the lights of the sky is condemned in many texts (cf. Deut. 4:19; 8:2; 17:2-5;
2 Kgs. 23:4-5,11; Jer. 8:2; 19:13; 32:29; Zeph. 1:5). The OT asserts several times that God created and controls
the heavenly lights (cf. Gen. 1:14-19; Ps. 19:1-6; Neh. 9:6). It is in connection with these texts
that "Lord of hosts" is a condemnation of idolatry (the worship of
gods/angels/spirits of the heavenly lights, cf. LXX of Deut. 32:8).

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.
